item.title: Ai2 Replaces Priority-Based GPU Scheduling with Hierarchical Fair-Share Budgeting System
item.description:
Ai2 Replaces Priority-Based GPU Scheduling with Hierarchical Fair-Share Budgeting System

The AI Infrastructure team at Ai2 has updated its compute management strategy by replacing a legacy priority-based scheduler with a system featuring GPU time budgets, hierarchical fair-share allocation, and a time-slicing contract. This new approach shifts resource management from case-by-case operational tasks to a transparent administrative process designed to handle demand that consistently exceeds available capacity by 2-3x.

🔍 Overview

Ai2 manages thousands of NVIDIA H100, B200, and B300 GPUs organized in clusters ranging from 88 to 1024 units. These resources support approximately 150 internal researchers working on diverse AI domains, including:

  • Full model flow for LLM and VLM training.
  • Robotics reinforcement learning (RL) simulation. 0* Post-training for scientific agentic use cases.

🧩 How it works

The new system is built on a hierarchy of needs designed to optimize distributed training workloads. Instead of solving a manual “knapsack problem” to fit research needs into a static schedule, leadership now allocates portions of GPU time in advance, allowing them to fund research efforts based on projected impact.

Level Component Description
Capstone Utilization The fraction of GPU capacity used over the lifetime of a workload.
Level 3 Impact How often the most valuable workloads are chosen to receive resources.
Level 2 Occupancy The fraction of available time assigned to a specific workload.
Foundation Availability How often the hardware is healthy and ready for work.

⚙️ Key details

The transition addresses several critical inefficiencies identified in the previous priority-based model:

  • Priority Inflation: Historically, 100% of scheduled workloads eventually used “HIGH” priority, starving lower-priority levels of GPU time.
  • GPU Squatting: Users previously parked “no-op” workloads to maintain access to resources, preventing others from launching real-time debugging tasks.
  • Maintenance Overhead: Because preemptability was optional, engineers spent significant time negotiating shutdowns for hardware maintenance.
  • Seasonality Issues: Previous attempts to assign GPU monopolies to specific teams caused resources to sit idle during natural lulls in research cycles.

💡 Why it matters

By moving to a time-budgeting model, Ai2 enables leadership to think like investors. Since research demand cannot be forecast with total precision due to the nature of novel science, the institute now decides how to fund research efforts before the workloads even exist. This ensures that every available GPU hour is allocated based on strategy rather than individual competition for scarce resources.

#AIinfrastructure #GPUclusters #Ai2 #MachineLearning #DistributedTraining

Source: Impactful scheduling for GPU clusters

item.title: SageMaker HyperPod integrates with Unified Studio and adds Spaces for governed GPU workloads
item.description:
SageMaker HyperPod integrates with Unified Studio and adds Spaces for governed GPU workloads

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod gives machine learning (ML) teams access to large pools of accelerated compute for training and fine‑tuning models. When several teams share a single cluster the technical setup is straightforward, but governance becomes the challenging part.

🔍 Overview

  • SageMaker HyperPod is a capability of Amazon SageMaker AI that provides purpose‑built infrastructure for foundation model training and inference at scale.
  • SageMaker Unified Studio is the data and AI development environment where teams build with their data and tools.
  • Unified Studio can connect a HyperPod cluster to a project, letting team members launch workloads, review cluster and task information, and open a JupyterLab workflow.
  • The integration keeps cluster management in SageMaker AI interfaces and APIs, allowing infrastructure teams to use established cloud‑operations processes while presenting approved compute to ML teams in their project context.

⚙️ Governance Model

  • Governance decisions include:
    • Which teams may use the cluster.
    • How much capacity each team receives.
    • How to handle competition for resources.
    • Who is accountable when usage drifts from policy.
  • When multiple teams share visibility into the same cluster, controls that govern who can do what become even more important.
  • A well‑governed environment separates:
    • Organizational administration
    • Project access
    • Cluster operations
    • Workload execution
  • Each layer answers a different question and uses different controls.

🏗️ Four Layers of Control

  1. Organization layer – identity and capacity policies that apply across the entire account.
  2. Project layer – collaboration boundaries defined in SageMaker Unified Studio (not strong runtime security boundaries).
  3. Cluster layer – AWS IAM, Amazon EKS, and Slurm controls that govern cluster‑level access.
  4. Workload layer – workload identity, data and KMS key policies, network policy, task‑view restrictions, and scheduler policy.

“A SageMaker HyperPod connection adds an approved cluster to a project. It doesn’t replace the cluster’s AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), or Slurm controls.”

All four layers must be aligned before the cluster is made available.

🧩 SageMaker Spaces on HyperPod

  • Earlier this year Amazon launched SageMaker Spaces for HyperPod, an add‑on that lets developers create interactive development environments directly on HyperPod EKS clusters.
  • Benefits:
    • Run JupyterLab or Code Editor environments without leaving the browser or using CLI tools.
    • Reduce time from cluster access to productive development to a few clicks.
    • Run interactive workloads alongside training jobs and model deployment, with support for fractional GPU allocations.
  • Management UI:
    • The new IDE and Notebooks tab on the HyperPod cluster detail page provides a complete user interface for Space management, removing the need for daily CLI commands.
    • Create Spaces with configurable compute, namespaces, storage, and HyperPod Task Governance for compute‑quota management via a guided form.
    • View all Spaces in a searchable table showing name, application type, status, access type, storage, GPU, and vCPU allocations.
    • Start or stop Spaces with a single selection to free compute when not in use.
    • Open Spaces directly in the browser (JupyterLab or Code Editor) or connect through a remote IDE such as VS Code.

🚀 Installing and Using Spaces

  1. Install the Spaces add‑on on the HyperPod EKS cluster from the SageMaker AI console → IDE and Notebooks tab. Choose Quick install (one‑click defaults) or Custom install (required for web UI access).
  2. Configure EKS access entries by attaching the managed policies:
    • AmazonSagemakerHyperpodSpacePolicy
    • AmazonSagemakerHyperpodUserClusterPolicy
    • AmazonSagemakerHyperpodSpaceTemplatePolicy to the IAM roles used by data scientists.
  3. Enable per‑user identity propagation on the Studio domain if it existed before the integration. This ensures each Studio user’s actions on the cluster are attributed in EKS access entries and AWS CloudTrail, enforcing strict Space ownership.
  4. Create and launch a Space:
    • In Studio, go to Compute → HyperPod, select the IDE and Notebooks tab.
    • After the Space status shows Running (a few minutes on a cold cluster, ~30–40 seconds with over‑provisioning), click Open to launch JupyterLab or Code Editor, or Open in VS Code for a remote IDE experience.

📚 Summary

  • By connecting SageMaker HyperPod clusters to Unified Studio projects, organizations can provide approved, high‑performance GPU compute to ML teams while retaining strong governance through four layered controls.
  • The new SageMaker Spaces UI gives data scientists a visual, click‑based workflow to create, manage, and use interactive development environments on the same HyperPod infrastructure that powers large‑scale training and inference.
  • This combination delivers a repeatable, governed model that separates infrastructure operations from project‑level development, enabling efficient use of shared GPU resources.

#SageMaker #HyperPod #MLOps #AIInfrastructure #MachineLearning

Source: Best practices for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod administration and governance | Amazon Web Services Source: Manage Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Spaces directly from SageMaker Studio | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Scalekit, Nebius, and Tenki Host Agents and Bagels Event for AI Founders
item.description:
Scalekit, Nebius, and Tenki Host Agents and Bagels Event for AI Founders

Scalekit, Nebius, and Tenki are hosting a special SF Tech Week edition of Agents & Bagels, a curated breakfast for founders and AI builders. The gathering is designed for individuals building production-grade agents and infrastructure to engage in high-signal networking over coffee and bagels.

🔍 Overview

The event focuses on bringing together people working across several specific domains in the AI ecosystem:

  • Agents
  • Developer tools
  • Infrastructure
  • Applied AI

⚙️ Key details

The breakfast gathering is structured to prioritize conversation over formal presentations.

  • Format: No panels, pitches, or long presentations.
  • Catering: Coffee and bagels provided for participants.
  • Access: Attendance is by approval only and invitations are non-transferable.
  • Media: Organizers may capture and distribute photos, videos, and audio recordings for promotional and marketing purposes.

🧩 How it works

The event is held in collaboration with several co-hosts and the Ugly Talk community.

Entity Role
Scalekit Co-host
Nebius Co-host
Tenki Co-host
Ugly Talk Event organizer and community platform

🚀 Availability

Participation is managed through a registration and approval process. Approved guests receive a confirmation email and a calendar invitation. Registration requires agreement to a Code of Conduct and a liability waiver. Attendees also agree to receive marketing communications from Ugly Talk and its partners, with the option to unsubscribe at any time.

💡 Why it matters

This gathering provides a venue for builders to share raw lessons and insights, following a model established by Ugly Talk in 2019 to transform business setbacks into breakthrough moments. It targets those scaling agent workflows and exploring next-generation AI infrastructure, offering a focused environment for peers in the ecosystem to start the day with meaningful conversations.

#SFTechWeek #AIAgents #AIInfrastructure #Startups

Source: UGLY TALK: AGENTS & BAGELS (BREAKFAST MEET UP FOR AGENT BUILDERS)

item.title: Microsoft expands biomimicry in data centers as AI growth raises community concerns
item.description:
Microsoft expands biomimicry in data centers as AI growth raises community concerns

Microsoft announced that it is expanding its use of “biomimicry” at data centers while facing increased pushback from local residents over construction, pollution, and noise.

🔍 Overview

  • Data centers have evolved from “relatively unassuming office buildings” in the early 2000s to massive “hyperscale” facilities spanning millions of square feet that house the physical infrastructure for AI.
  • Communities across the United States are protesting the impact of these facilities on quality of life, pollution, water, and electricity bills.
  • Tech companies, including Microsoft, have responded with promises to mitigate harm by paying for infrastructure upgrades needed in local water and power systems.

🌱 Biomimicry Strategy

  • “Biomimicry is sort of a catch‑out term for many of the ways technologies take inspiration from nature, from ‘painless’ needles that imitate a mosquito’s proboscis to naturally ventilated buildings modeled after termite mounds.”
  • Microsoft describes its approach as “blending our datacenters into the natural landscape” to “create resilient ecosystems that support biodiversity, strengthen community ties, and help our datacenters become better neighbors.”
  • The company is adding more gardens and native trees on‑site and investing in “400+ acres of woodland and pollinator prairie restoration” with the goal of leaving the land “more productive than we received it.”
  • It is also funding projects that repair damaged ecosystems, such as a $4.2 million creek‑restoration effort in 2023 and outfitting stormwater ponds with forebays to prevent sediment escape.

📍 Local Impact – San Antonio

  • San Antonio City Councilmember Ric Galvan recalls the first data centers in his city and notes that there are now “more than a dozen data centers in Galvan’s roughly 55‑square‑mile district,” with an expectation of around 20 if proposed projects are completed.
  • In 2022, Microsoft cut down more than 2,600 trees across a 33‑acre site to build a data center, sparking controversy over loss of canopy that helps mitigate heat.
  • Residents have complained about traffic, tree removal, constant bright lights, and noise that “concentrate nuisances in the same neighborhoods.”
  • Galvan said, “that [feeling] gets taken away pretty quickly when you make a gigantic data center.”
  • He added, “Maybe … they’re trying to just make sure that they’re covering their bases,” and, “but also, I think if that’s the case, that’s fine,” provided Microsoft and other operators address concerns around pollution, water use, and destruction of green spaces.

📈 Scale & Reach

  • Microsoft operates “more than 300 data centers in more than 34 countries.”
  • The company started biomimicry projects at a data center in the Netherlands in 2022.
  • It now plans to bring “nature‑inspired solutions to restore and enhance natural ecosystems” to more than 20 sites in the US and Germany, and to apply the same approach to all new projects in the US and a growing number worldwide.
  • In the United States, Microsoft is repurposing the shuttered Foxconn LCD‑factory property in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin, for its own data centers.

🤝 Community Response & Mitigation

  • Across the country, communities are rising up against hulking data warehouses.
  • Microsoft’s stated mitigation includes ecosystem restoration, woodland and prairie projects, and customized habitat‑enhancing solutions for each site.
  • According to a Microsoft spokesperson, the company is “investing in enhancement projects that includes 400+ acres of woodland and pollinator prairie restoration” with the aim of leaving land “more productive than we received it.”

🔧 Key Facts

  • Hyperscale data centers now span millions of square feet and power AI workloads.
  • More than a dozen data centers exist in San Antonio’s 55‑square‑mile district; projected growth to ~20 centers.
  • Microsoft is spending “hundreds of millions of dollars” to build several new data centers in the Greater San Antonio area.
  • Biomimicry initiatives involve on‑site gardens, native trees, ecosystem restoration, and stormwater management.
  • Microsoft operates >300 data centers in >34 countries and has launched biomimicry projects in the Netherlands, the US, and Germany.
  • Community concerns focus on traffic, noise, light pollution, tree loss, heat mitigation, and water usage.

#Microsoft #Biomimicry #DataCenters #AIInfrastructure

Source: If a data center is camouflaged in the woods, will anyone hate it?

item.title: Kevin O’Leary’s Utah “Wonder Valley” Data Center Project Stalls After Political Backlash
item.description:
Kevin O’Leary’s Utah “Wonder Valley” Data Center Project Stalls After Political Backlash

🔍 Overview

  • Kevin O’Leary announced plans to build the world’s biggest data center in Utah.
  • The project is technically called Stratos, but it is more prominently known as Wonder Valley.

📏 Key Details

  • Size: 40,000 acres of land.
  • Power: Nine gigawatts, more than double the average power usage of the entire state of Utah.
  • Intended as an AI campus, billed as the largest data center in the world.
Name Alias
Stratos Wonder Valley

🏛️ Political & Legal Fallout

  • The proposal upended Utah politics and created a political firestorm that stopped the project.
  • Approval was pursued through the Military Installation Development Authority (MIDA), a state agency that can override local land‑use decisions and act like a municipal government for its project areas.
  • MIDA’s authority would have accelerated permitting, zoning, and other regulations.
  • Local residents were kept in the dark, leading to anger that ultimately halted the development.
  • O’Leary called his critics “Chinese spies” on Fox News, resulting in a defamation lawsuit; Fox News later issued an on‑air apology.

🔄 Aftermath

  • The land originally slated for Wonder Valley is now being used for a Microsoft data center.
  • The episode highlights broader themes: the AI industry’s infrastructure boom, bipartisan backlash to such build‑outs, and the challenge of local democracy that even massive financial resources cannot easily overcome.

#AIInfrastructure #DataCenters #UtahPolitics #KevinOLeary

Source: How Utah locals fought Kevin O’Leary’s AI data center

item.title: Shifting AI Economics from Consumption Pricing to Infrastructure Ownership
item.description:
Shifting AI Economics from Consumption Pricing to Infrastructure Ownership

As AI transitions from experimental pilots to production portfolios, enterprises are evaluating whether to continue using consumption-based pricing or treat AI infrastructure as a productive asset.

🔍 Overview

AI is moving into production portfolios comprising assistants, agentic applications, and retrieval-and-knowledge systems. According to Deloitte’s 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise, worker access to AI rose 5% in 2025, and the number of companies with at least 40% of their AI projects in production is expected to double within six months.

⚙️ Key details

While consumption pricing provides flexibility and limits commitment, it can create variable monthly costs that are difficult to forecast as workloads and model requirements change. Organizations face a “crossover point” where owning capacity becomes more economical than buying it one request at a time.

Factors influencing this crossover point include:

  • The models being used
  • Balance of input and output tokens
  • Performance requirements
  • System design
  • Energy costs
  • The required operating model

🧩 How it works

Different AI workloads create distinct cost profiles:

Workload Type Cost Profile Characteristics
Retrieval-heavy knowledge systems May process far more context for every interaction compared to simple assistants
Agentic workflows May involve repeated reasoning, retrieval, model calls, and tool use for a single business task

When multiple workloads share infrastructure, enterprises can spread fixed costs across more productive use to improve the economics of ownership.

💡 Why it matters

Moving toward owned capacity allows a business to manage AI as a strategic infrastructure investment rather than a fluctuating monthly spend. However, this requires an operating model to ensure capacity creates value by:

  • Bringing users and workloads on board quickly
  • Governing AI use
  • Reviewing utilization
  • Identifying underutilized capacity
  • Continually identifying high-value use cases

#AIEconomics #EnterpriseAI #AIInfrastructure #CloudComputing

Source: Making AI an asset, not an expense

item.title: NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS Enables Higher GPU Density via Dynamic Power Sharing
item.description:
NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS Enables Higher GPU Density via Dynamic Power Sharing

NVIDIA and Nscale have evaluated DSX MaxLPS, a system that uses policy-governed power sharing to dynamically allocate power across resources, allowing customers to deploy up to 40% more GPUs within the same approved power budget.

💡 Why it matters

AI factories operate within a hierarchy of electrical limits, including utility service, substations, power-distribution equipment, racks, nodes, and GPUs. Traditional static power planning reserves enough power for every node to reach its specified peak simultaneously. However, AI workloads rarely draw constant power:

  • Training workloads: Move through compute, communication, synchronization, and checkpointing.
  • Inference workloads: Alternate between prefill, decode, memory-bound work, network activity, and idle intervals.
  • Variable requests: Even identical models draw different power based on concurrencies and request shapes.

Static reservations prevent unused capacity in one reservation from being applied to another node, leaving valuable infrastructure underused during normal operation.

🧩 How it works

DSX MaxLPS combines chip, system, thermal, and software technologies to maximize output within land, power, and shell (LPS) constraints. The Dynamic Power Software provides the control layer for the following process:

  • Infrastructure Mapping: Operators organize nodes into a managed group with an aggregate power budget.
  • Telemetry Collection: The system collects power telemetry from GPUs, nodes, racks, and groups at intervals sufficient to detect emerging power events and available headroom.
  • Policy Governance: Operator-defined rules establish group and node limits, allocation priorities, reserve requirements, and emergency or maintenance responses.
  • Dynamic Allocation: When some resources draw less than their allocation, the software adjusts GPU power limits so other resources can use that capacity, while maintaining the aggregate budget.

⚙️ Key details

A joint evaluation of this approach was conducted at Nscale’s data center at the Verne campus in Keflavík, Iceland, which is powered entirely by renewable energy. The technical walkthrough utilized the following configuration:

Component Detail
Systems NVIDIA GB300 NVL72
GPUs NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra
Workload Kimi K2.5 in FP4
Software NVIDIA Dynamo and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM
Sequence Length 8K input / 1K output
Workload Mix High-throughput and low-latency inference instances

#NVIDIA #DataCenter #GPU #EnergyEfficiency #AIInfrastructure

Source: How NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS Maximizes AI Factory Throughput and Efficiency | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA Releases Topograph Open Source Toolkit for Topology-Aware GPU Scheduling
item.description:
NVIDIA Releases Topograph Open Source Toolkit for Topology-Aware GPU Scheduling

NVIDIA has introduced Topograph, an open source toolkit designed to identify cluster network topology to enable workload managers to make topology-aware scheduling decisions.

💡 Why it matters

AI factories are power-limited systems that require full optimization to deliver maximum value. Because GPUs exchange data continuously during training and inference, distributed workloads benefit from communication locality. Poor workload placement can lead to:

  • Fragmented topology domains
  • Increased traffic across shared links
  • Reduced throughput and higher job costs
  • GPUs consuming provisioned power while waiting for data without advancing the workload

Topograph prevents these bottlenecks by mapping how cluster hardware is connected, allowing schedulers to favor nearby resources and avoid spreading tightly coupled workloads across distant domains.

🧩 How it works

Topograph solves the problem of maintaining an accurate view of GPU and fabric relationships as a cluster changes. It uses two primary concepts:

  • Providers: These discover topology from cloud APIs or on-premises systems and normalize it into a canonical model.
  • Engines: These translate the normalized model into formats expected by various workload managers.

Within the NVIDIA DSX OS cluster orchestration layer, Topograph works alongside KAI Scheduler and Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) to enable topology-aware gang scheduling.

⚙️ Key details

Topograph supports a variety of hardware and software integrations to ensure the scheduler works from current data rather than a manually maintained snapshot.

Component Supported Integration/Requirement
Cloud Providers Google Cloud, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale, and OCI
On-Premises Providers InfiniBand (with ibnetdiscover), NetQ (for Spectrum-X or Multi-Node NVLink domains)
Engines/Outputs Kubernetes node labels, Slurm topology configuration, Slinky ConfigMaps, Node Feature Discovery (NFD) resources, instance-oriented topology JSON
Slurm Engine Requires a writable volume for its configured topology.conf output path
NFD Engine Requires the alpha NodeFeatureGroupAPI feature gate
Crusoe Provider Runs in Kubernetes; reads fabric and accelerator-domain labels from Crusoe Managed Kubernetes nodes

🚀 Availability

Topograph is an open source toolkit with an open provider interface, allowing operators to add and contribute providers for their own environments upstream. As of September 16, 2026, the toolkit supports various provider-to-engine output combinations, though requirements may vary by version and configuration.

#NVIDIA #GPU #Kubernetes #Slurm #AIInfrastructure

Source: Topology-Aware Workload Scheduling with NVIDIA Topograph | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA FLARE 2.9 Introduces Slurm Support for Flexible Federated Learning Job Execution
item.description:
NVIDIA FLARE 2.9 Introduces Slurm Support for Flexible Federated Learning Job Execution

NVIDIA FLARE now enables federated learning (FL) deployments across heterogeneous infrastructure through a two-layer architecture that separates federation management from job execution. This design allows participating sites to retain local control over compute resources while maintaining secure federation coordination.

🔍 Overview

NVIDIA FLARE addresses the challenge of running FL jobs across diverse environments by decoupling persistent federation services from job execution. This separation lets each site use its preferred execution backend—Docker, Kubernetes, or Slurm—within the same federation.

🧩 How It Works

  • Two-layer architecture:
    • Persistent layer: Long-running parent processes manage federation state, authenticate connections, and coordinate work.
    • Execution layer: Transient job workers handle submitted FL tasks.
  • When a job is submitted, each site’s parent process launches a worker via its configured platform (Docker/Kubernetes/Slurm).
  • Jobs specify resource requirements (GPUs, CPUs, memory) separately from platform details. Each site’s launcher translates these into platform-specific allocations.

⚙️ Key Details

Supported Execution Backends:

Platform Key Capabilities
Docker Single-host execution (workstations/edge systems); parent/job containers; GPU exposure via NVIDIA Container Toolkit
Kubernetes Helm-deployed parent pods; job pods scheduled with CPU/GPU/memory requirements; supports namespaces, secrets, persistent volumes
Slurm Submit jobs as batch tasks; supports bare execution, Pyxis/Enroot, Apptainer; enforces Slurm policies (QoS, partitions)

Site Control: Each site chooses its runtime and retains authority over:

  • Compute allocation
  • Datasets, images, secrets
  • Scheduling policies
  • Resource enforcement

🚀 Availability

  • Docker/Kubernetes support introduced in FLARE 2.8
  • Slurm support added in FLARE 2.9

💡 Why It Matters

This architecture enables large-scale federated learning across organizations with differing infrastructure. Sites maintain autonomy over resources and security policies while participating in collaborative model training. The platform-agnostic design simplifies federation setup and allows efficient resource utilization.

#NVIDIA #FederatedLearning #AIInfrastructure

Source: Scaling Federated Learning Across Docker, Kubernetes, and Slurm with NVIDIA FLARE | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Hostinger Launches GPU Hosting for AI Development
item.description:
Hostinger Launches GPU Hosting for AI Development

Hostinger has introduced GPU Hosting, providing direct access to NVIDIA GPUs with a deployment process designed to be simpler than traditional hyperscalers.

⚙️ Key details

Users maintain control of the server environment through full root, terminal, and SSH access. To streamline setup, the service allows for the launch of preconfigured AI applications that include necessary drivers, containers, and dependencies.

Management and usage monitoring are handled via the Hostinger dashboard, and live availability is displayed before deployment.

💰 Pricing and Billing

Hostinger uses an hourly credit model that meters GPU usage per minute with no long-term commitment. Key billing details include:

  • Continuous Billing: Charges continue as long as the instance exists, including during idle periods.
  • Stopping Charges: Destroying the instance is currently the only way to stop compute charges.
  • Data Transfer: There are no egress charges for transferring generated data out of the instance.

🚀 Availability

There are currently six instance options across five GPU models:

item.title: Google to Invest €13 Billion in AI Infrastructure and Nuclear Power in Finland
item.description:
Google to Invest €13 Billion in AI Infrastructure and Nuclear Power in Finland

Google has announced a €13 billion ($15.1 billion) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, marking the company’s largest single investment in the EU to date. This initiative includes a massive deal to purchase nuclear power in the Nordic country over the next two decades.

⚙️ Key details

Scheduled for disbursement in 2027 and 2028, the investment will support Google’s map, search, and chatbot services through the following projects:

  • Data centers
  • Electrical grid improvement
  • Clean energy and battery projects

Google is expanding its existing site in Hamina and opening data center operations in three new municipalities:

Location Action
Hamina Expanding site on a “remarkable level”
Kajaani Opening data center operations
Muhos Opening data center operations
Vaala Opening data center operations

💡 Why it matters

Economic and Employment Impact Google claims the investment will create 37,000 jobs (7,000 permanent and the remainder during construction) and contribute approximately €3.6 billion to Finland’s GDP.

Energy Infrastructure To manage energy needs, Google has entered a purchase agreement for 50% of the energy output from one of Finland’s two nuclear power plants for the next 22 years. Regarding this “bring your own power” (BYOP) strategy, Ruth Porat, Google President and Chief Investment Officer, noted, “This is Google’s first nuclear energy deal outside of the United States.”

Operational Continuity Plant operator Fortum stated that this deal allows the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant to continue operating until its licenses end in 2050; otherwise, the plant—which provides about 10% of Finland’s electricity—would not have been able to operate past 2030. Following the news, Fortum shares rose 15.5% to their highest level in over four years.

Energy Demand Network operator Fingrid forecasts a 40% jump in energy consumption over coming years due to Finland’s data center boom.

#Google #Finland #AIInfrastructure #NuclearEnergy #DataCenters

Source: Finland: Google announces €13 billion AI, energy investment

item.title: Codex Pooler launches as a self-hosted gateway for Codex-compatible agents
item.description:
Codex Pooler launches as a self-hosted gateway for Codex-compatible agents

Codex Pooler has been introduced as a self-hosted gateway designed for running Codex-compatible agents, tools, and automation through stable Pool API keys.

🔍 Overview

Codex Pooler connects clients to upstream accounts while maintaining a stable access key interface. The gateway supports different configurations depending on the number of accounts:

  • Single upstream Codex account: Provides credential isolation, client normalization, metadata-only operations, and saved reset visibility.
  • Multiple upstream accounts: Added to provide shared capacity and routing across eligible accounts.

🧩 How it works

Clients send familiar Codex backend or OpenAI-compatible requests to the gateway. While upstream assignments, lifecycle states, reset policies, and capacity change behind the scenes, the external Pool key remains stable.

When a request is made, Codex Pooler selects an eligible account based on the following criteria:

  • Model support
  • Quota evidence
  • Limits
  • Session continuity
  • Routing policy
  • Health

⚙️ Key details

Operators and administrators are provided with specific control surfaces to manage their environments securely.

Administration Roles

  • Instance owners: Maintain the global administration surface.
  • Instance admins: Work exclusively with their assigned Pools.

Operator Management

Operators get a single centralized place to manage Pools, accounts, API keys, saved resets, routing, request accounting, audit logs, and health. This management is conducted without storing:

  • Prompts
  • Files
  • Audio
  • Images
  • Bearer tokens
  • Raw Codex secrets

#CodexPooler #DeveloperTools #AIInfrastructure #SelfHosted

Source: icoretech/codex-pooler

item.title: Saudi Arabia unveils $15 B AI and cloud infrastructure push at LEAP 2026
item.description:
Saudi Arabia unveils $15 B AI and cloud infrastructure push at LEAP 2026

At LEAP 2026 in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia announced a multi‑billion‑dollar surge of AI‑related investments, partnerships, and infrastructure launches, signaling the Kingdom’s move into a new phase of its technology strategy.

🔍 Overview

  • LEAP 2026 highlighted the Kingdom’s expanding digital economy across cloud, AI, telecom, venture capital, and skills development.
  • By the end of the opening day, more than $15 billion in AI and advanced‑technology launches, investments, and partnerships had been announced.
  • The initiative is framed as part of a broader, ambitious technology strategy built around artificial intelligence, advanced infrastructure, national talent, and an investment ecosystem.

💰 Investment totals by day

  • Day 1: > $15 B across AI, cloud, data centers, semiconductor, energy, and industry‑specific applications.
  • Day 2: > $2.5 B aimed largely at expanding data‑center capacity and advanced‑technology infrastructure.
  • Day 3: $857 M in technology and manufacturing investments, including cloud infrastructure and data‑center manufacturing projects.

☁️ Cloud & AI infrastructure milestones

  • AWS Saudi Cloud Region – on track to launch December 2026, representing $5.3 B in planned cloud‑infrastructure investment.
  • The region will let developers, startups, government entities, and companies run workloads from Saudi data‑centers.
  • AWS‑HUMAIN partnership – plans up to 50 MW of capacity in Saudi Arabia’s first AI Zone by 2028, using AWS Trainium chips and NVIDIA infrastructure.
  • HUMAIN’s Arabic LLM “ALLAM” to become available via Amazon Bedrock; the HUMAIN Fabric data platform will be offered through AWS Marketplace.

🤝 Partnerships and platform expansions

  • DataVolt + HUMAIN – jointly developing 100 MW of the first 360 MW phase of an AI‑ready data centre at Oxagon in NEOM; the first 100 MW expected 2028.
  • AMD, Cisco, HUMAIN – production AI computing infrastructure now live, powered by AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs, and Cisco networking. Plans for an additional 250 MW beginning 2027, targeting 1 GW of AI infrastructure by 2030.
  • HUMAIN AI Cloud – powered by NVIDIA HGX B300 Blackwell Ultra systems, currently delivering 1.1 MW of operational AI capacity with >90 % utilization; slated to expand to 35.1 MW by 2027.
  • Strategic investment in Arabic.AI and Tarjama – to boost Arabic‑language translation, document intelligence, and enterprise AI capabilities (translation management, digitizing legacy archives, AI agents for contracts, tenders, filings).
  • Reflection AI partnership – deploying Reflection’s first generally available model on HUMAIN infrastructure later this year, with joint work on model customization, sovereign AI deployment, and compute for future training.
  • KORA Systems collaboration – co‑developing HUMAIN OS, an AI‑native Linux operating system that interprets user intent to select the appropriate model, application, or environment.

📊 Capacity roadmap

Initiative Capacity (MW) Target year Notes
AWS AI Zone (with HUMAIN) 50 2028 Uses AWS Trainium chips & NVIDIA infrastructure
HUMAIN AI Cloud (NVIDIA) 1.1 (operational) → 35.1 2027 Current utilization >90 %
DataVolt‑HUMAIN Oxagon phase 1 100 (first tranche) 2028 Part of 360 MW NEOM AI‑ready data‑center phase
AMD/Cisco/HUMAIN joint venture up to 250 additional (on top of existing) 2027 Aim for up to 1 GW AI infrastructure by 2030

🌍 Why it matters

  • The Kingdom’s technology ambitions are framed around measurable impact on people: better connectivity and faster digital services.
  • Building AI‑ready infrastructure, localized large‑language models, and an ecosystem of partners positions Saudi Arabia to develop home‑grown AI products and companies with global reach.
  • The massive investment in cloud and AI hardware creates a foundation for talent development, venture capital activity, and downstream industry applications across energy, manufacturing, and services.

item.title: Tech Giants Invest 15 Billion Dollars in AI Infrastructure at LEAP 2026
item.description:
Tech Giants Invest 15 Billion Dollars in AI Infrastructure at LEAP 2026

The opening days of LEAP 2026 in Riyadh have resulted in approximately $15 billion in investments, partnerships, and computing infrastructure agreements. Held under the theme “Into New Worlds,” the fifth edition of the conference highlights Saudi Arabia’s ambition to build and export technology. Major global tech companies have deepened their commitments to the region, focusing on sovereign cloud, AI infrastructure, and physical logistics.

🔍 Overview

Much of the early dealmaking involves HUMAIN, a Public Investment Fund-owned AI company. The organization is expanding partnerships across cloud infrastructure and personal technology to support training and inference workloads. The Kingdom is working toward a goal of having up to 1 gigawatt of AI infrastructure in place by 2030.

⚙️ Key details

Partner Project/Infrastructure
Amazon Web Services (AWS) $5.3 billion investment for a cloud infrastructure region and a 50MW AI Zone.
AMD & Cisco Deployment of MI355X and next-generation MI400 Series GPUs for GPU-as-a-service.
Microsoft Expansion of HUMAIN ONE AI productivity service and a new cloud data center region.
stc group Development of 250MW AI-ready data center capacity and global connectivity networks.
Qualcomm Launch of the Horizon Ultra AI PC powered by the Snapdragon X2 Elite platform.
HP Launch of HP Garage 2.0, a startup incubator for Vision 2030 solutions.

🧩 How it works

  • AI Computing: AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and Cisco networking technology are currently operational, allowing HUMAIN to provide GPU-as-a-service for model training.
  • Cloud Regions: Microsoft’s Saudi Arabia East region will include three availability zones to improve latency, security, and business continuity for government and private-sector organizations.
  • AI Productivity: HUMAIN ONE is hosted on Azure and provides a single interface for enterprise applications. It integrates Microsoft 365 Copilot and HUMAIN’s ALLAM models to support Arabic-language agents.
  • Hardware Integration: The Horizon Ultra AI PC uses an 18-core Qualcomm Oryon CPU, Adreno GPU, and Hexagon NPU to distribute workloads between local processing and cloud infrastructure.

🚀 Availability

  • Current: AMD Instinct MI355X infrastructure is now operational and in use by HUMAIN customers.
  • September 2026: HUMAIN’s AI PC is scheduled for release to enterprise customers.
  • November 2026: Microsoft’s cloud data center region in Saudi Arabia East is expected to open.
  • December 2026: AWS expects to open its first cloud infrastructure region in the Kingdom.
  • 2027: Deployment of AMD’s MI400 Series GPUs and the introduction of HUMAIN OS for the Horizon Ultra device.
  • 2028: Up to 50MW of capacity is expected to be available in Saudi Arabia’s first AI Zone.

💡 Why it matters

stc Group CEO Olayan Alwetaid stated that the Kingdom is undergoing “a rapid transformation in the field of artificial intelligence.” The various infrastructure projects, such as the AWS investment and the 1GW goal for 2030, are designed to support local data storage, lower latency, and the expansion of digital services across the Middle East and Africa.
